commentary.bottom_line: Three studies tested integration, and each found lower burden or higher use when the AI tool sat inside the EHR, PACS, or main monitor, but none had a concurrent comparator in routine practice. Ten hazard studies consistently link separate interfaces to low use, which suggests the problem is real while the size of any benefit from integration remains uncertain.

perspectives.view: Two pre-post studies without concurrent comparators and one simulation with 23 clinicians test the practice. Caries risk assessment completion rose from under 5% to a peak of 89% after EHR integration, and 93.3% (14/15) of clinicians reported that PACS-integrated AI did not interfere with practice. Risk of bias, small samples, and indirectness lower certainty to very low.

In a simulation, a secondary monitor raised NASA-TLX physical demand by 17.33 points and frustration by 14.33 points compared with an overlay on the main surgical monitor. Strain was reported by 60% versus 6.7%. Hazard studies name separate EHR tabs and external platforms as barriers, and 67% of staff rarely or never used one unintegrated tool.

None of the three tests measured diagnostic errors, missed findings, or patient harm. With a separate referral platform, only 28% of referral records were complete and 44.4% of feedback was reviewed. This suggests information may be lost at handoffs, but no study shows that integration closes that gap.

No test reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. An endorsing framework describes EHR integration at an FQHC network, but that account does not measure outcomes. Whether integration changes use or burden for clinicians serving these patients has not been tested.

No study reported integration cost, build time, vendor dependence, or staffing needs. The caries risk assessment gains appeared over roughly 20 months after the July 2022 launch, which may indicate that benefits accrue slowly. One operational guide proposes a quick standalone front end for pilots before EHR integration, and no study has tested that tradeoff.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares the same AI tool delivered inside versus outside the EHR or PACS with a concurrent control. Stepped-wedge or cluster designs that measure use, clinician time and workload, errors, patient outcomes, and integration cost would address this, and they should include safety-net settings.
commentary.underserved_note: None of the three tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The settings were Chinese hospitals, a US dental program, and a Canadian surgical simulation. The findings may not transfer to under-resourced sites, where EHR build capacity and vendor support can differ.
